analysis.one_liner: Lets banks keep fund holdings the Volcker Rule would otherwise force them to sell.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote on April 29, 2014, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died in the Senate Banking Committee when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill carves an exception out of the Volcker Rule — the post-2008 rule that bars banks from owning interests in hedge fund and private equity style investment vehicles. Regulators read that ban to cover certain debt holdings in collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), which are securities made up mostly of business loans, because those holdings carry a right to fire the fund's manager. The bill says such CLO debt is not a forbidden fund ownership, and bars the rule from forcing banks to sell CLO debt issued before early 2014 until July 2017. It passed the House but never got a Senate vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks that already owned CLO debt would avoid having to sell it on the rule's schedule, sparing them potential losses from a wave of simultaneous sales. The investment firms that manage CLOs keep their bank buyers. The bill's title frames the benefit as flowing to American employers, on the argument that CLOs are a channel for business lending and that forced bank sales would disrupt it.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars the Volcker Rule from being construed to require divestiture, before July 21, 2017, of any debt securities of collateralized loan obligations issued before January 31, 2014.

It declares that a bank is not considered to have a forbidden ownership interest in a CLO merely because it holds a debt security whose only control right is the ability to participate in removing or replacing the fund's investment manager for cause.

It writes a specific definition of removal 'for cause' for CLO investment managers into the rule, covering breaches of contract, inability to perform, materially harmful conduct, and events threatening debt holders' interests.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on the rule the bill amends. The Volcker Rule was written to keep banks that benefit from federal deposit insurance out of hedge-fund-style investing; narrowing it means banks keep these fund-like holdings longer, and any losses on them land more on the banks rather than being wound down on the rule's original schedule. The cost to the public is indirect and modest.

drawbacks.text: The bill narrows a core Dodd-Frank restriction: the Volcker Rule treats these fund-like holdings, including CLO debt with manager-removal rights, as exactly the ownership interest the ban was meant to cover.
Extending the divestiture deadline to July 21, 2017 delays the risk reduction the rule intended, leaving banks exposed to losses on bundled business loans for longer than the rule as written allowed.
A good-faith objection from the other side is that the measure is narrow: it covers only CLO debt already issued by early 2014, and the divestiture requirement still returns after July 2017.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stakes are small on both sides. Banks holding legacy CLO debt faced a real cost if they had to sell on the rule's timetable, and the bill's reading — that a passive debt holding with a manager-removal right is not fund ownership — is a defensible one that even the underlying rule's drafters had to grapple with. Against that, the bill chips at a rule designed to keep insured banks away from fund-style risk. Because it passed the House but died in the Senate, neither the benefit nor the cost was realized through this bill.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote, but the Senate Banking Committee never acted on it before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The House Financial Services Committee ordered the bill reported, as amended, by a vote of 53 to 3 on March 14, 2014.
The House passed the bill, as amended, by voice vote on April 29, 2014, under a procedure reserved for bills expected to pass with broad agreement.

The Senate received the bill on April 30, 2014 and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where no further action was recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill had one Democratic cosponsor in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the Volcker Rule as written stayed in force for banks holding CLO debt, with the divestiture requirement and the firewall against fund-style ownership intact. Banks with legacy CLO holdings did not get the statutory relief, though no one bore a new cost either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The rule as written stayed in force

for.name: Rep. Andy Barr
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt legacy CLO debt from the Volcker Rule's divestiture requirement.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a markup and ordered the bill reported, as amended, 53 to 3.

for.name: Rep. Scott Garrett
for.what_they_did: Moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill on the House floor on April 29, 2014.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 30, 2014 and took no recorded action on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The House committee reported it 53 to 3 and the full House passed it by voice vote with a Democratic cosponsor; no opposition is recorded anywhere in the action history.

industries.note: The bill would have spared banks from being forced to sell legacy CLO debt until July 2017, avoiding potential losses from sales made all at once. The public cost is that this weakens a rule meant to keep insured banks away from fund-style investments — modest here, because the carve-out is narrow and time-limited.

Managers of collateralized loan obligations and similar funds keep their bank buyers and gain a codified definition of when they can be removed for cause. Their gain comes from loosening a bank-safety restriction rather than from anything that costs the public directly.

industries.industry: Business borrowers in the leveraged loan market
industries.note: The bill's title frames the point of the bill as preserving financing for American employers, on the argument that CLOs bundle business loans and that forced bank sales would disrupt that lending. The title is a claim of purpose, not an established effect.
